summary:
Manitoba stands under the national framework: Canada is among the safest large destinations for trans visitors, with gender identity and gender expression protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code as added by Bill C-16 in 2017. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincially, the Manitoba Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The NDP government has a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Code to gender expression as well, which Justice Minister Matt Wiebe said would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing; the bill was scheduled for debate later in 2025. Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba, welcomed the amendment.

Manitoba's recorded hate-crime exposure is low relative to the rest of the country. Statistics Canada's police-reported hate-crime release of 30 March 2026 records 4,882 incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba posted the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000 alongside Newfoundland and Labrador and recorded no increase in 2024, placing it among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly across the country, and police figures capture only reported incidents.

Manitoba has enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level. The legislature passed a bill on 30 May 2024 recognising March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender; Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

Provincial observance of trans commemorations is established. On 20 November 2023 Manitoba again raised the transgender flag in Memorial Park in Winnipeg for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance first marked eight years earlier, with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine and Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing.
tangentialFactors:
The proposed addition of gender expression to the Manitoba Human Rights Code is framed by the provincial government as an alignment measure, bringing the province into line with most other provinces rather than departing from them; until the bill passes, gender expression is not a named ground in Manitoba's Code even though gender identity is.

Manitoba's low hate-crime rate sits against a national picture in which police-reported hate crime has risen over the longer arc and in which an LGBTIQ+ organisation, Egale Canada, publishes analysis of national police hate-crime data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations. The national total of 4,882 incidents in 2024 and the 12.1 per 100,000 national rate give the provincial figure of 5.3 per 100,000 its comparative context.

Two provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans residents, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and parental notification. These govern residents rather than visitors, but they mark a direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes and are the backdrop against which Manitoba's expansion of protection is being pursued.

The bill before the Legislative Assembly would add gender expression to that Code, extending coverage to preferred pronouns and to outward appearance such as clothing in employment, services and housing.

Residents have provincially enacted recognition of trans and two-spirit visibility: the Legislative Assembly passed a bill on 30 May 2024 designating March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, sponsored by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature.

The provincial government marks the Transgender Day of Remembrance publicly, raising the transgender flag in Memorial Park in Winnipeg, most recently on 20 November 2023, eight years after the observance was first marked. Ministers Nahanni Fontaine and Uzoma Asagwara have stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Local advocates, including Anastasia Gibson of Brandon, use the occasion to record deaths from transphobic violence and to state that such violence shows no sign of slowing.

Trans Manitoba, led by executive director Charlie Eau, is the provincial advocacy organisation engaged with the legislative amendment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the gender-expression amendment is unresolved on the available sources: they record a government bill before the Legislative Assembly scheduled for debate later in 2025, but do not confirm final passage or assent.

The Egale Canada 2024 hate-crime analysis report could not be retrieved; the link does not resolve. The report is understood to be an LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of national police hate-crime data including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations, but its specific findings are not sourced here.

No trans-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or court litigation for Manitoba appears in the inventory. The Statistics Canada figures are police-reported and capture only incidents that were reported and recorded, so they understate actual incidence; the 5.3 per 100,000 figure is a provincial rate and does not disaggregate gender-identity or gender-expression motivations for Manitoba.
